Optimization Interview Lab

"Our reef scene takes 40 ms a frame on the target. We need 60 fps. Walk me through it." The interviewer has a capture and will hand it over if you ask. Choose each move, and see where the frame ends up and how the answer is scored.

One frame, five moves. Goal: reach 16.7 ms or less and a strong hire, 18 of 20 or more.

Lesson 078: optimization interview questions

    What this shows

    Ask for data first

    A list of tricks says you've read about optimization. Asking for a capture says you've done it. Interviewers usually have one ready.

    Predict, then test

    "If the pair checks are quadratic, halving the fish should cut them to a quarter." A prediction you can check is worth more than a confident guess.

    The bottleneck moves

    Fix the slowest stage and another one becomes slowest. Saying "now I'd measure again" is part of the answer.

    This lab is a model, not a real hiring rubric. It uses Lesson 078's numbers for one reef frame on the target: game thread 40 ms (fish proximity checks 25, physics 5, animation 4, other 6), render thread 14, GPU 18. The frame is the slowest stage (Lesson 075). Micro-optimizing cuts proximity 25 → 9, physics 5 → 3, animation 4 → 2; a better algorithm cuts proximity 25 → 1 (a grid), physics 5 → 2 (sleeping bodies), animation 4 → 1 (lower update rate far away). Without a capture, "the slowest stage" is a guess: the GPU, 18 → 14. Measuring again after a fix moves on to the new slowest stage once: the GPU, 18 → 16 (water particle overdraw). Scorecard: five parts, 0 to 4 each.
